title: Layout system & custom layouts
scopeHtml: Constraints model, single-pass measurement, Layout/MeasurePolicy, intrinsics, sub-composition cost, Box/Row/Column/FlowRow/ConstraintLayout, alignment lines, inspection, custom layout and text measurement performance. (Research basis: developer.android.com custom layouts, intrinsic measurements, flow layouts, ConstraintLayout pages. Library-version specifics are marked "verify".)

questions.promptHtml: How does Compose decide how big a composable is? Explain constraints.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every layout bug (stretched divider, crash in scrollables, "my fillMaxWidth does nothing") is a constraints bug. This separates people who guess from people who reason.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Parent passes down a Constraints object: minWidth, maxWidth, minHeight, maxHeight. The child picks a size inside that range and reports it up. Parent then places the child. So sizes flow up, constraints flow down. Modifiers like size, fillMaxWidth, padding mostly just rewrite the constraints before the child sees them.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Layout of each node is three steps: measure children, decide own size, place children. Constraints is a packed value class holding four ints (pixels). maxWidth can be Constraints.Infinity (unbounded). A bounded constraint with min == max is a "fixed" constraint.

Parent constraints  : minW=0   maxW=1080  minH=0 maxH=Infinity
  Modifier.fillMaxWidth()  -> minW=1080 maxW=1080   (forces min up to max)
  Modifier.width(200.dp)   -> minW=maxW=600 (at 3x density), clamped to parent range
  Modifier.padding(16.dp)  -> child gets maxW reduced by 2*48px, then adds it back to own size

Key rules: a child must obey the constraints it receives (sizes are coerced). fillMax* sets min = max; wrapContent/default leaves min = 0 so child can be smaller. Modifiers earlier in the chain see the parent's constraints; later ones see the already-modified ones (ordering details belong to the modifiers section). An unbounded max means "as big as you want", which is why fillMaxHeight() inside an infinite-height scroll container behaves as wrap.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Probe() {
    Box(Modifier.size(200.dp)) {                       // child constraints: 0..600px (3x density)
        Box(Modifier.fillMaxSize())                    // min=max=600px -> fills
        Box(Modifier.size(400.dp))                     // asks 1200px, coerced to 600px (size() respects parent)
        Box(Modifier.requiredSize(400.dp))             // ignores parent, overflows, centered
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking size(400.dp) always wins; it is clamped by the incoming constraints, requiredSize is the one that breaks them.
  • Reasoning in dp instead of px; constraints are pixels.
  • Forgetting unbounded constraints exist (scrollables, wrapContent-style containers).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does Constraints.Infinity mean for a child? → No upper bound; child can size to content. Scrollables pass it on their scroll axis.
  2. Difference between size and requiredSize? → size coerces into parent constraints; requiredSize measures child with exact constraints regardless and then positions it centered in the parent's reported size.
  3. How is this different from View MeasureSpec? → MeasureSpec: EXACTLY/AT_MOST/UNSPECIFIED plus one size; Compose uses explicit min/max ranges per axis, which is a superset and removes the ambiguity of match_parent vs wrap_content.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "parent tells child max size". Senior: min/max ranges in px, modifiers as constraint transformers, infinity handling, requiredSize escape hatch, and how this removes View's double-measure pass.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: "Why is my image stretched in the lazy list" and "fillMaxHeight does nothing" tickets are almost always an unbounded or already-fixed constraint upstream.

questions.promptHtml: What are Box, Row and Column really doing, and how do fillMaxSize, wrapContentSize and align interact inside them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know the primitives well enough to predict layout without trial and error.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Box stacks children and aligns them using contentAlignment or per-child Modifier.align. Row/Column place along a main axis in order, with Arrangement for main-axis spacing and Alignment for the cross axis. By default they wrap their content up to the incoming max; fill modifiers force min = max.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Row/Column are Layouts implemented as one shared RowColumnMeasurePolicy. Pass 1 measures non-weighted children with unbounded main-axis max (min 0); pass 2 divides leftover space among weighted children. Cross-axis size = largest child (or fills if constrained to fill).
  • Box measures every child with the incoming constraints (min relaxed to 0 unless propagateMinConstraints = true), box size = max of children (or the incoming min if forced). matchParentSize() in Box scope sizes a child to the box without contributing to the box size, unlike fillMaxSize(), which is part of what determines box size.
  • Arrangement.SpaceBetween etc. only matter if the Row has extra main-axis space, i.e. its constraints are bounded and larger than its content, usually with fillMaxWidth().

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Box(Modifier.size(120.dp)) {
    Image(painter, null, Modifier.matchParentSize())          // background, doesn't grow the box
    Text("Live", Modifier.align(Alignment.BottomEnd))
}
Row(Modifier.fillMaxWidth(), horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.SpaceBetween,
    verticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically) { Text("A"); Text("B") }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Arrangement.SpaceBetween on a wrap-content Row: nothing happens.
  • Using fillMaxSize() on a background child inside a wrap-content Box: it can push the Box to parent size; use matchParentSize().
  • Expecting Alignment on Column to align on the main axis.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can't Row center children vertically with Arrangement? → Arrangement is main axis only; cross axis uses Alignment.Vertical.
  2. What is propagateMinConstraints? → Passes Box's min constraints to children so a child can be forced to fill a fixed-size Box.
  3. How many measure passes does Row do? → Each child measured once; weights just defer the weighted children until leftover space is known (not a re-measure).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior knows the unweighted-first/weighted-second order and matchParentSize semantics, and can predict results without running the preview.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "full-bleed banner" pushed its parent card to full screen height because the scrim used fillMaxSize in a wrap-content Box.

questions.promptHtml: Compose forbids measuring a child twice. Why, and what does that buy and cost you versus the View system?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The key architectural reason Compose can handle deep hierarchies; a senior must connect it to performance and to intrinsics.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each node is measured at most once per layout pass with one set of constraints, so layout cost is linear in node count. The View system could measure children multiple times (RelativeLayout, LinearLayout with weights, nested weights), and nesting multiplied that into exponential behavior. The cost: you can't "try one size, then another"; if you need info before measuring, you use intrinsics or sub-composition.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
In Views, a parent calling measure() repeatedly on children, with each child doing the same, gives O(2^depth) in worst cases, which is why a flat ConstraintLayout was recommended. Compose enforces the rule at runtime: calling measurable.measure() twice on the same measurable in one measure pass throws IllegalStateException. Because each node is measured once, deep nesting costs only O(n). The official guidance states that deep layout hierarchies are handled efficiently, which is why flattening is not a concern in Compose the way it was in Views.

Escape hatches, in increasing cost:

  1. Intrinsics: ask min/maxIntrinsicWidth/Height of a child before measuring (a separate, query-only traversal).
  2. SubcomposeLayout: compose children lazily during measure so you can use measured sizes to decide what to compose.
  3. Measure with different constraints in separate layout-modifier nodes (each measures once).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Layout(content) { measurables, constraints ->
    val first = measurables[0].measure(constraints)
    // measurables[0].measure(constraints.copy(maxWidth = 100)) // throws: measured twice
    layout(first.width, first.height) { first.place(0, 0) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing a nested Row/Column tree is slow. It isn't; recomposition scope and unneeded intrinsics are the real costs.
  • Calling measure in a loop for "best fit" sizing in a custom layout.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you size a divider to the tallest sibling then? → IntrinsicSize.Min on the Row.
  2. Does the runtime exception always fire? → Yes for same measurable in the same pass (verify exact message per version); the intent is a hard rule.
  3. Does single-pass mean Compose never re-lays out? → No: layout reruns when constraints or state read in measure/layout change, but each run is single-pass per node.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior ties this to why ConstraintLayout's flat-hierarchy advantage mostly evaporates, and lists intrinsics and subcompose as the sanctioned workarounds with their costs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team ported nested-weight View XML to Compose without a perf regression and stopped "flattening" code in reviews.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through writing a custom Layout. What is MeasurePolicy, and when would you use the layout modifier instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can go beyond stock layouts, and understand measure/place scopes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Layout(content, modifier, measurePolicy) takes the children as measurables; in the policy I measure each child with chosen constraints, compute my size, call layout(w, h) { ... }, and place each placeable inside that lambda. MeasurePolicy is the interface wrapping that lambda plus the four intrinsic functions. The layout modifier is the same idea for a single child: modifies how one composable is measured and placed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• MeasureScope.measure(measurables, constraints): MeasureResult. Measurable.measure(constraints) returns a Placeable, which has a width/height and alignment-line values.
  • layout(width, height, alignmentLines) { placeable.placeRelative(x, y) }. Placing happens in PlacementScope, which is the layout phase; reads of state inside the placement lambda re-run placement only (not measure).
  • Use placeRelative to auto-mirror in RTL; place for absolute.
  • Pass content once; if you need distinct slots, either use Modifier.layoutId or call Layout with contents: List<@Composable () -> Unit> (multi-content overload, check your version) or SubcomposeLayout.
  • layout modifier: one child, good for baseline padding, aspect-ratio tricks, offsets with layout-phase reads.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Stack(modifier: Modifier = Modifier, content: @Composable () -> Unit) =
    Layout(content, modifier) { measurables, constraints ->
        val loose = constraints.copy(minWidth = 0, minHeight = 0)
        val ps = measurables.map { it.measure(loose) }
        val w = constraints.constrainWidth(ps.maxOfOrNull { it.width } ?: 0)
        val h = constraints.constrainHeight(ps.sumOf { it.height })
        layout(w, h) {
            var y = 0
            ps.forEach { it.placeRelative(0, y); y += it.height }
        }
    }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting to coerce size with constrainWidth/Height (size outside constraints is silently clamped or misbehaves).
  • Forgetting to place a child: it is measured but invisible.
  • Creating a new MeasurePolicy object each recomposition for heavy layouts; remember it when it captures parameters.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why placeRelative? → Layout direction mirroring.
  2. Where do you read animated state to avoid remeasure? → Inside the placement block or a graphicsLayer lambda.
  3. How do you give a custom layout intrinsics? → Override the four intrinsic functions in an explicit MeasurePolicy; defaults are approximations.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions constraint coercion, RTL, placement-scope state reads, and intrinsic overrides without being asked.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom chip layout rendered nothing in one release because a conditional branch skipped place.

questions.promptHtml: How does Modifier.weight work in Row/Column, and how does it differ from fillMaxWidth?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Common source of truncated or overflowing UI.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Weight divides the remaining main-axis space after non-weighted children are measured, in proportion to weights. fillMaxWidth() demands the whole incoming max width for that child. Mixing them wrongly lets the fill child eat everything.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Row measures unweighted children first (main-axis max = remaining), subtracts their size, then for each weighted child gives remaining * weight / totalWeight as an exact (or fill = false: max-only) main-axis constraint. So a long unweighted Text can starve weighted siblings. weight(1f, fill = false) lets the child be smaller than its share.

With FlowRow the weight is computed per line, not over all items (official docs).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Row(Modifier.fillMaxWidth()) {
    Icon(Icons.Default.Star, null)                       // measured first, fixed
    Text(title, Modifier.weight(1f), maxLines = 1, overflow = TextOverflow.Ellipsis)
    Text(price)                                          // unweighted: measured first, never truncated
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Modifier.weight(1f) on a child in a scrollable (infinite main axis) container: no meaning, throws or misbehaves; weight needs bounded main axis.
  • fillMaxWidth() on the first of two children, starving the second.
  • Forgetting fill = false for a bubble that should hug its content up to a cap.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is price visible while title truncates here? → Unweighted measured first.
  2. weight vs fillMaxWidth(0.5f)? → fraction of the incoming max width of the Row, not of remaining space after siblings.
  3. Behavior in Column inside verticalScroll? → Unbounded height; weights have no space to split, avoid.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior explains the two-phase order and designs for text expansion.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Localized strings (long German) pushed the price off-screen until the title was weighted and the price left unweighted.

questions.promptHtml: What are intrinsic measurements and why do they exist if Compose forbids double measurement?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Classic "does this person know the layout contract" question.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Intrinsics let a parent query a child's preferred min/max width or height without measuring it, so it can compute constraints before the single real measurement. Example: Row(Modifier.height(IntrinsicSize.Min)) makes a divider as tall as the tallest text.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Four queries: minIntrinsicWidth(h), maxIntrinsicWidth(h), minIntrinsicHeight(w), maxIntrinsicHeight(w). IntrinsicSize.Min means the smallest size at which content still paints correctly (for Text height, the height at the given width; for width, the width of the longest word per line break rules); Max is the size beyond which more space doesn't help (Text: single-line width).

Official docs: asking for intrinsics doesn't measure children twice; children are queried before they are measured. The Row's minIntrinsicHeight is the max of children's min intrinsic heights; the divider's is 0, so it then fills the height the Row computed.

Cost: intrinsics are a separate recursive traversal of the subtree, and since each level may query its children for multiple values the cost compounds with depth. Use sparingly, never on a huge subtree.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Row(Modifier.height(IntrinsicSize.Min)) {
    Text("Hi", Modifier.weight(1f))
    VerticalDivider(Modifier.fillMaxHeight().width(1.dp))
    Text("There, a much longer line that wraps", Modifier.weight(1f))
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Applying IntrinsicSize at the root of a big screen "to fix alignment".
  • Assuming all layouts support intrinsics; SubcomposeLayout (so BoxWithConstraints, Scaffold, lazy lists) does not (verify; reported in secondary sources and throws).
  • Writing a custom Layout with default intrinsic approximations and getting wrong sizes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Alternatives to a divider matching height? → Custom layout or Modifier.drawBehind using measured size.
  2. Why does it fail around a LazyColumn? → Lazy layouts use subcomposition and can't answer intrinsics.
  3. How do you implement them in a custom layout? → Override intrinsic functions consistently with measure (see custom layout notes).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior states the cost model (extra traversal) and the SubcomposeLayout limitation, and offers a custom-layout alternative.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A settings screen with IntrinsicSize.Min on each of 40 rows added ~1.2 ms to layout each frame in a trace; moving it to only the three rows that needed it fixed it (illustrative composite).

questions.contextHtml:
A product detail screen shipped with this code. It crashes in QA on every open (crash-free sessions dropped to 0% on the internal build; 100% of 12 testers). Logcat: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Vertically scrolling component was measured with an infinity maximum height constraints, which is disallowed. One of the common reasons is nesting layouts like LazyColumn and Column(Modifier.verticalScroll()).

@Composable
fun ProductScreen(reviews: List<Review>) {
    Column(Modifier.fillMaxSize().verticalScroll(rememberScrollState())) {
        ProductHeader()
        LazyColumn { items(reviews) { ReviewRow(it) } }   // 300 reviews
        Footer()
    }
}

A teammate suggests wrapping the LazyColumn in Modifier.height(2000.dp). Another says "add fillMaxHeight()".
questions.promptHtml: Why does it crash, and what is the right fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Compose doesn't allow nested scrolling, set a fixed height." Fixed height makes content clip or leave a gap on other devices and defeats laziness; fillMaxHeight does nothing under infinite constraints.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must the header and footer scroll with the reviews (one scroll surface)? How many reviews, paged? Is the screen also used in a tablet pane?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident but a blocker: remove the nested scroll today by making the screen a single LazyColumn.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) verticalScroll passes unbounded max height; LazyColumn demands bounded height on its scroll axis. Red herring: the 300 items (it would also crash with 3).
  4. How I'd verify: The exception text names it; reproduce in a preview with 3 items.
  5. Root cause: verticalScroll measures its content with maxHeight = Infinity. LazyColumn needs a finite viewport to decide how many items to compose; with infinity it'd have to compose everything, so it throws instead of silently doing so.
  6. Fix:
LazyColumn(Modifier.fillMaxSize()) {
    item { ProductHeader() }
    items(reviews, key = { it.id }) { ReviewRow(it) }
    item { Footer() }
}
  1. Prevention: Lint/review rule: no scrollable inside same-axis scrollable; test with a screenshot test including a long list.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a fixed height (breaks on font scale / device sizes); not heightIn(max=) unless the list is genuinely short and non-lazy (then a plain Column with forEach is honest about eager composition of 300 rows).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the inner list is horizontal? → Different axis is fine: LazyRow in a vertical scroll works since its height is wrap-content.
  • Header must be sticky? → stickyHeader in LazyColumn (check experimental status in your foundation version).
  • Reviews load in pages? → Same LazyColumn, add a loading item; keys keep scroll position.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An engineer "fixed" this with height(5000.dp) and the footer floated 3 screens below the content on a tablet; support tickets read "huge blank area".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fixed height hack, cannot explain infinity.
  • Hire: single LazyColumn with item blocks, explains unbounded max.
  • Strong hire: also discusses eager vs lazy composition cost, keys, and why the exception exists.

questions.promptHtml: What happens when a child wants to be larger than its parent allows? Compare size, requiredSize, wrapContentSize and sizeIn.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests deep understanding of how modifiers rewrite constraints and where overflow/centering comes from.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: size coerces the requested size into the parent's constraints. requiredSize ignores them, so the child can overflow and is centered in the space the parent gave. wrapContentSize relaxes the min constraints so content can be smaller than the slot and aligned inside it. sizeIn sets min/max bounds that are still coerced to the incoming range.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Incoming minWidth=maxWidth=300px (a fixed slot): a child Box(Modifier.size(100.dp)) would still be 300px because the parent forces it; to be 100.dp inside the slot use wrapContentSize(Alignment.Center).size(100.dp) (wrapContentSize first resets min to 0).
  • requiredSize(400.dp) measures the child at exactly 1200px (3x density); the node reports a size clamped to constraints but the child is placed centered, overflowing visually, and may be clipped by the parent's clip/hit tests.
  • Typical Material usage: minimumInteractiveComponentSize() uses requiredSizeIn to guarantee a 48dp touch target even in a smaller parent.
slot 300px fixed, child asks 100px
  size(100)                  -> 300px (parent wins)
  wrapContentSize().size(100)-> 100px, centered
  requiredSize(500)          -> child 500px, overflows slot

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Box(Modifier.size(100.dp)) {                      // slot
    Icon(painter, null, Modifier.requiredSize(48.dp)) // 48dp target even in 100dp slot, fine
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Setting size and wondering why a weighted or fill parent overrides it.
  • Using requiredSize for general sizing; neighbors don't know the child overflows (overlap, clipping).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does Modifier.size(300.dp).size(100.dp) resolve? → The second is coerced into the first's constraints (300), so the outer wins: 300. Order matters.
  2. Why does Material use requiredSize-style min touch targets? → Accessibility 48dp while visual stays small.
  3. Does overflow receive touches outside the parent bounds? → Hit-testing is bounds-based on the layout node; overflow outside parent bounds may not receive pointer input (verify per version).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior can compute the resulting px from the constraints and knows the min-reset role of wrapContentSize.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 24dp icon button in a toolbar failed accessibility scanner (target < 48dp) until the min-interactive modifier was restored after a custom wrapper removed it.

questions.promptHtml: What are alignment lines in Compose and when would you use them? How do baselines work?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks knowledge of layout beyond bounding boxes; common for text-and-icon alignment.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An alignment line is a named coordinate along an axis that a composable exposes after measurement; FirstBaseline and LastBaseline are built in. Parents like Row with Alignment.Top/Bottom/CenterVertically use bounding boxes, but Modifier.alignByBaseline() or paddingFromBaseline align on text baselines.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Placeable[FirstBaseline] returns the offset (px) or AlignmentLine.Unspecified. A layout can publish custom lines via layout(w, h, alignmentLines = mapOf(MyLine to y)). Parents read those lines (e.g. Row + Modifier.alignBy(MyLine) / alignByBaseline() aligns children so their lines coincide, and sizes the cross axis to fit the displacement). Lines propagate upward through single-child layouts like padding, so a Text inside Box still reports its baseline.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Row {
    Text("Total", style = labelStyle, modifier = Modifier.alignByBaseline())
    Text("$128", style = bigStyle, modifier = Modifier.alignByBaseline())  // baselines match
}
// official example: Modifier.paddingFromBaseline(top = 32.dp)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Centering a small label next to a large number with CenterVertically and getting visibly misaligned text.
  • check(placeable[FirstBaseline] != Unspecified) in custom modifiers; non-text children don't have it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do custom lines get exposed? → alignmentLines map in layout(...).
  2. Where do baselines come from for Text? → Text layout result; first/last line.
  3. Do lines survive multiple wrappers? → They propagate through layouts that forward them (standard modifiers do).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior knows the API and can fix baseline alignment in a price row and spec-matching (e.g. 24sp from top to first baseline).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Designer-reported "price looks 2dp off" fixed with alignByBaseline instead of hand-tuned offsets that broke at large font scales.

questions.promptHtml: What does SubcomposeLayout do, and why is BoxWithConstraints considered expensive?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of composition vs layout phases and cost trade-offs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Normally composition runs fully before layout. SubcomposeLayout lets you compose some content during measurement, using information (constraints or sibling sizes) only known then. BoxWithConstraints is built on it so its content lambda can read maxWidth. The cost is composing during layout: extra composition work per constraints change, no intrinsics, and defeated skipping.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Phases: composition → layout → draw. Subcomposition creates a child composition inside the measure pass via subcompose(slotId, content) returning measurables. Lazy lists, Scaffold and BoxWithConstraints use it. Consequences:

  • Content is recomposed whenever incoming constraints change (e.g. during a window resize or an animated size), since the lambda receives them.
  • Subcomposition work happens in the layout phase on the main thread; jank shows as long Compose:layout slices in traces.
  • Intrinsics unsupported (verify).
  • Slot reuse: SubcomposeSlotReusePolicy governs recycling (used by LazyLayout prefetch).

Rule: use BoxWithConstraints only when the composition tree must differ by size (e.g. 1-pane vs 2-pane). If you only need the size for layout math, use Layout/layout modifier or Modifier.onSizeChanged carefully. For window size classes use currentWindowAdaptiveInfo() / calculateWindowSizeClass at the top, not per item.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
BoxWithConstraints {
    if (maxWidth < 600.dp) CompactLayout() else ExpandedLayout()
}
// cheaper when you only need a measurement-time decision:
Layout(content) { ms, c -> /* branch on c.maxWidth here */ layout(c.maxWidth, 0) {} }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping every list item in BoxWithConstraints.
  • Using BoxWithConstraints for something Modifier.fillMaxWidth(fraction) or aspectRatio can do.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does BoxWithConstraints content not skip as usual? → Its lambda has a scope receiver of constraints and is invoked in measure; changes in constraints force re-invocation.
  2. How do you measure cost? → Perfetto/system trace slices of layout; Layout Inspector doesn't show subcompose directly.
  3. Implement a "header sized to its tallest slot" without it? → Custom Layout with multiple layoutId children; no subcompose needed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior can name the composition-during-layout cause and picks an alternative (window size classes, Layout).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: See the list-scale incident in the next question; a chat app's frame time dropped after replacing a subcompose-based layout with a plain Layout (reported in a public engineering write-up; I could not verify exact figures).

questions.contextHtml: Feed screen, 2.1M DAU, mid-tier Android devices (4 GB RAM) account for 55% of sessions. After a release that "made cards responsive", p95 frame time while scrolling went from 11 ms to 24 ms; JankStats shows 14% janky frames (was 3%). Crash rate and memory unchanged. Release diff: each FeedCard is now wrapped in BoxWithConstraints { val compact = maxWidth < 360.dp ... }; an image loader library was also bumped; and a new analytics event fires per item impression. Perfetto trace of a janky frame shows a long Compose:layout section containing nested Compose:recompose slices.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Disable the analytics", "add remember everywhere", or blame the image loader without trace evidence.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is jank correlated with the release only on certain devices? Does the card width actually vary across items (list in one column)? Can we flag-rollback? Is the problem only during first scroll (new items) or also steady state?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back via the feature flag or ship a hotfix reverting the wrapper; staged rollout to 5% to confirm p95 returns toward 11 ms.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) BoxWithConstraints per item causes composition inside the layout pass for each new item and creates a subcomposition per card; (b) image loader bump (check decoding thread); (c) analytics event on impression doing work on main; (d) overdraw. The trace slices make (a) most likely; (b)/(c) are red herrings unless traces show them.
  4. How I'd verify: Perfetto with androidx.tracing / Compose tracing enabled; compare traces release vs previous; bisect by removing the wrapper only; Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric scrolling test A/B; Layout Inspector to confirm card widths are identical for all items.
  5. Root cause: Every card subcomposes in measure, so first-time composition of each card moved from composition (can be prefetched/amortized by lazy prefetch) into layout where it blocks the frame; constraints identical across items made the work pure overhead.
  6. Fix: Short-term: compute compact once from the list's width (one BoxWithConstraints or window size class above the list) and pass a boolean down. Long-term: card is a fixed layout with fillMaxWidth().
val compact = LocalConfiguration.current.screenWidthDp < 360 // or WindowSizeClass
LazyColumn { items(feed, key = { it.id }) { FeedCard(it, compact) } }
  1. Prevention: Macrobenchmark scroll test in CI with p95 budget; code review rule "no BoxWithConstraints in item content"; baseline profiles.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't remove responsiveness; move it up a level. Don't micro-optimize remember calls before the trace identifies the cost.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Card width really does vary (grid with different spans)? → Pass span count as a parameter from the grid scope, which already knows it.
  • Foldable resize mid-scroll? → The single top-level read recomposes once; acceptable.
  • Cannot rollback? → Hotfix with the hoisted boolean, flag it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team spent two sprints on image caching before a trace showed 70% of layout time was subcomposition.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random micro-optimizations.
  • Hire: identifies BoxWithConstraints in items via trace and hoists it.
  • Strong hire: explains composition-during-layout, builds benchmark gate, evaluates alternatives.

questions.promptHtml: When would you use FlowRow, and how do its weights, maxItemsInEachRow and fractional sizing differ from Row?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Replaces the old "write a custom wrap layout" interview question; checks API awareness and nuances.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: FlowRow lays items left to right and wraps to a new line when they don't fit, ideal for chips/tags. maxItemsInEachRow caps items per line. Weights are per line, and fillMaxWidth(fraction) is a fraction of the whole container, not remaining space as in Row.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per the official docs: main axis arrangement via horizontalArrangement, cross axis via verticalArrangement; Modifier.align aligns within a line; fillMaxRowHeight() makes items in one line equal height (fillMaxColumnWidth() for FlowColumn). Weight example: lines of 1f,2f,1f,3f share leftover space of that line by weight * remaining / total. With 10 items and maxItemsInEachRow = 3 and weight(1f), the last lone item takes the full line. API status: it started behind @OptIn(ExperimentalLayoutApi::class) (foundation 1.5); verify whether your foundation version has it stable. Also see platform docs for FlexBox/Grid mentioned in recent adaptive guidance (verify availability).

FlowRow isn't lazy: all items are composed and measured, so for hundreds of chips use a lazy grid.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@OptIn(ExperimentalLayoutApi::class)
@Composable
fun Tags(tags: List<String>) = FlowRow(
    horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(8.dp),
    verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(8.dp),
    maxItemsInEachRow = 4
) { tags.forEach { AssistChip(onClick = {}, label = { Text(it) }) } }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using FlowRow for 500 items (non-lazy).
  • Expecting a global weight across lines.
  • Modifier.weight + long text creating uneven lines.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you show "+3 more" overflow? → maxLines / overflow parameters exist in newer foundation versions with ContextualFlowRow (verify version).
  2. How do you create equal-width grid? → maxItemsInEachRow + weight(1f) on every item, accepting the last-line stretch.
  3. How would you implement it yourself? → Custom Layout: measure children loose, accumulate widths per line, wrap at maxWidth, place line by line.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior knows per-line weights, the non-lazy limit, and when to hand-write a layout.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A filter sheet with 300 locations ran FlowRow and janked on open; switched to LazyVerticalGrid with adaptive cells.

questions.promptHtml: You wrote a custom Layout. A parent uses IntrinsicSize.Min around it and the result is wrong. Why, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who have shipped custom layouts from those who've copied the docs example.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: When you don't override intrinsics, the framework approximates them using default behavior, which may not match what your measure does. Fix: implement MeasurePolicy as an object and override the intrinsic functions so they mirror measure: e.g. for a vertical stack, minIntrinsicHeight(width) is the sum of the children's minIntrinsicHeight(width).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The official page says custom Layout/layout modifier intrinsics are calculated automatically from approximations and may be wrong; override minIntrinsicWidth, minIntrinsicHeight, maxIntrinsicWidth, maxIntrinsicHeight in MeasurePolicy (or the LayoutModifier equivalents). The contract: each must be consistent with measure. For a padding modifier: subtract vertical padding from the incoming height before asking the child for width, then add horizontal padding; guard Constraints.Infinity.

Cost: intrinsic queries recurse the subtree (no placeables). Large unbalanced trees queried at several levels get repeatedly traversed; keep intrinsic functions O(children) and cheap.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
object StackPolicy : MeasurePolicy {
    override fun MeasureScope.measure(ms: List<Measurable>, c: Constraints): MeasureResult { /* sum heights */
        val ps = ms.map { it.measure(c.copy(minHeight = 0)) }
        return layout(c.constrainWidth(ps.maxOfOrNull { it.width } ?: 0), c.constrainHeight(ps.sumOf { it.height })) {
            var y = 0; ps.forEach { it.placeRelative(0, y); y += it.height }
        }
    }
    override fun IntrinsicMeasureScope.minIntrinsicHeight(ms: List<IntrinsicMeasurable>, width: Int) =
        ms.sumOf { it.minIntrinsicHeight(width) }
    override fun IntrinsicMeasureScope.minIntrinsicWidth(ms: List<IntrinsicMeasurable>, height: Int) =
        ms.maxOfOrNull { it.minIntrinsicWidth(height) } ?: 0
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Overriding only min and not max, then using IntrinsicSize.Max.
  • Not handling Constraints.Infinity inputs.
  • Intrinsics that disagree with measure after later edits.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you test? → Unit test layouts with compose-ui-test and compare IntrinsicSize modifier result vs expected px.
  2. Do you need intrinsics at all? → Only if parents will query; most leaf-level custom layouts never are.
  3. What if your layout can't answer cheaply? → Don't support; document, or avoid IntrinsicSize above it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior knows the defaults are approximations and treats intrinsics as part of the layout's API contract.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An in-house TagLayout produced clipped chips inside a Modifier.width(IntrinsicSize.Max) dialog until intrinsics were implemented.

questions.contextHtml:
A reviewer finds this custom "badge on corner" layout in a PR. QA reports: in Arabic (RTL) the badge sits on the wrong corner; on small phones the content is sometimes clipped at the bottom; once in a while a crash appears in a stack: IllegalStateException: Measurable ... already measured.

@Composable
fun Badged(modifier: Modifier = Modifier, content: @Composable () -> Unit) {
    Layout(content, modifier) { ms, c ->
        val main = ms[0].measure(c)
        val badge = ms[1].measure(c)
        val again = ms[0].measure(Constraints.fixed(main.width, main.height)) // "make sure it's exact"
        layout(c.maxWidth, c.maxHeight) {
            main.place(0, 0)
            badge.place(main.width - badge.width / 2, -badge.height / 2)
        }
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: List every defect and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Only notices RTL.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should the badge overflow the bounds? Is the content always two children? Where does the badge need to be placed with RTL?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Block the merge; no production exposure yet.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked / defects: (a) double measure of ms[0] violates single-pass (crash); (b) place instead of placeRelative breaks RTL; (c) reporting c.maxWidth/maxHeight makes the layout fill parent (clip/overlap; maxHeight may be Infinity inside a scroll, huge crash risk); (d) negative y places badge outside bounds, clipped by parent; (e) ms[1] crashes if one child.
  4. How I'd verify: Preview with @Preview(locale = "ar"), small-device preview, a test in a scroll container.
  5. Root cause: Not honoring the measure/place contract: measure once, coerce size, use relative placement, size from the measured content.
  6. Fix:
Layout(content, modifier) { ms, c ->
    require(ms.size == 2) { "Badged expects main + badge" }
    val loose = c.copy(minWidth = 0, minHeight = 0)
    val main = ms[0].measure(loose)
    val badge = ms[1].measure(loose)
    val w = c.constrainWidth(main.width + badge.width / 2)
    val h = c.constrainHeight(main.height + badge.height / 2)
    layout(w, h) {
        main.placeRelative(0, badge.height / 2)
        badge.placeRelative(main.width - badge.width / 2, 0)
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Previews in LTR/RTL/font-scale; a layout test; lint-style review checklist (constrain, placeRelative, single measure).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not wrapping in try/catch the exception; not using requiredSize hacks. Alternative: Box + Modifier.offset with BadgedBox from Material (exists in M3) if no custom behavior is needed.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not fillMaxSize in layout? → Never grow beyond content unless asked; infinite constraints crash.
  • Does offset change layout size? → No, it only moves placement.
  • Cross-axis alignment lines? → Pass alignmentLines if needed.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite app shipped an RTL regression in checkout that only affected Arabic markets and showed up as a 6% conversion gap.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: finds one defect.
  • Hire: finds measure-twice, RTL, constraints.
  • Strong hire: also finds infinite-constraints and child-count risks, proposes BadgedBox.

questions.promptHtml: Should you use ConstraintLayout in Compose? How does it differ from nested Row/Column/Box?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you carry View-era dogma ("flatten everything") into Compose and know current guidance.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In Views, ConstraintLayout reduced nesting because nested measure was costly. In Compose, deep hierarchies are cheap because of single-pass measurement, so ConstraintLayout offers less. It's still useful for complex relational layouts (barriers, chains, guidelines) and decoupled ConstraintSets. Note: the current Android docs page carries a deprecation notice for constraintlayout-compose (verify against your target library version), steering to Row/Column/Box, custom layouts, and newer adaptive layouts.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
From the docs: the DSL uses createRefs(), constrainAs(), linkTo(), parent; decoupled API uses ConstraintSet + layoutId; guidelines, barriers, chains. The docs themselves say Spacers can replace guidelines, intrinsics can replace barriers, and Arrangements can replace chains. Costs: an extra dependency with separate versioning, constraint solving per layout pass, and relationships that don't compose with lazy lists well. Benefit: one flat container for a dense form where elements relate across rows, and animated constraint sets (MotionLayout, also marked deprecated).

Decision guide:

Linear/simple relationships        -> Row/Column/Box
Equal heights / sibling-dependent  -> IntrinsicSize or custom Layout
Dense cross-referenced, designer-given constraints, migrating XML -> ConstraintLayout (accept dependency)
Wrapping chips                     -> FlowRow

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
ConstraintLayout(Modifier.fillMaxWidth()) {
    val (avatar, title, sub) = createRefs()
    Image(painter, null, Modifier.size(48.dp).constrainAs(avatar) { start.linkTo(parent.start); top.linkTo(parent.top) })
    Text(name, Modifier.constrainAs(title) { start.linkTo(avatar.end, 12.dp); top.linkTo(avatar.top) })
    Text(role, Modifier.constrainAs(sub) { start.linkTo(title.start); top.linkTo(title.bottom) })
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping a whole screen in ConstraintLayout "for performance".
  • Using ConstraintLayout inside every lazy item.
  • Ignoring the library's deprecation note when starting new code.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Equivalent of a barrier? → Intrinsics or a custom layout.
  2. Why did View-era perf advice stop applying? → Single-pass measurement.
  3. How would you migrate a 600-line XML ConstraintLayout? → Do it per component; start with Row/Column/Box, reserve ConstraintLayout for the few truly relational pieces.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior rejects the "ConstraintLayout is faster" myth, cites the docs' own guidance, and weighs maintenance cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A migration kept a ConstraintLayout for one 20-element card; trace showed no benefit over nested layouts and the card was later rewritten in Row/Column for readability.

questions.contextHtml: A 12-engineer team is migrating the 38-screen XML app (ConstraintLayout everywhere) to Compose incrementally; 4.5M MAU, 40% on devices with 3 GB RAM. A tech lead proposes: "keep ConstraintLayout in Compose to port XML 1:1 and avoid perf risk". First ported screen (order summary, 90 elements) shows p95 frame 17 ms during an animated expand, up from 12 ms in XML; app startup unchanged. The ported code uses constraintlayout-compose with ConstraintSets swapped on expansion, plus BoxWithConstraints to choose sets.
questions.promptHtml: How do you decide the approach and fix this screen?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Compose is slower, keep the XML screens" or "ConstraintLayout is always the fastest".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is jank only during the animation or at rest? Release build with baseline profile? Does the 1:1 port matter for design parity? How often do designers change this screen?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship behind a flag; XML screen stays as fallback.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) debug build/no baseline profile (red herring until ruled out); (b) per-frame ConstraintSet swap re-solves the entire 90-element system each animation frame; (c) BoxWithConstraints recomposition as the size animates; (d) recomposition of all 90 children from a hoisted animation float.
  4. How I'd verify: Release+R8 macrobenchmark A/B, Perfetto trace of the animation; Layout Inspector recomposition counts; compiler reports for unstable params.
  5. Root cause (typical): the animated progress is read in composition, so the whole constraint system is rebuilt and re-solved per frame, and subcomposition sits above it.
  6. Fix: Read animation in layout/draw (e.g. graphicsLayer {}, Modifier.layout), animate only the section that changes using AnimatedVisibility/animateContentSize on a simple Column, and decide the set once outside the animation. Use ConstraintLayout only for the dense 20-element header.
  7. Prevention: Team guideline: default to Row/Column/Box; ConstraintLayout needs a justification; macrobenchmark gate in CI for ported screens.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't ban ConstraintLayout (docs flag a deprecation, verify; but it still works) and don't rewrite all 38 screens first; port screen by screen, measure each.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Designers deliver constraint-based specs from Figma? → Translate relationships to Row/Column/Box; use Compose layout idioms.
  • Mixed XML/Compose screens (ComposeView)? → Keep ConstraintLayout in XML parts until ported; interop cost small.
  • Dependency risk? → Constraint library versions are separate; pin and audit.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found that most 1:1 ports were faster once ConstraintLayout was replaced by 3-level nested Rows; the "flat is faster" assumption was a View-era reflex.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: dogmatic either way.
  • Hire: measures, explains why flat isn't needed, moves reads out of composition.
  • Strong hire: sets migration policy, benchmark gate, and rollback.

questions.promptHtml: How do you keep a custom layout fast? What belongs in composition, measure, and placement?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests phase awareness and allocation hygiene, a senior-level concern for scroll-critical custom layouts.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Do as little as possible per measure; avoid allocations (lists, maps, lambdas) in the measure block; read frequently changing state in the placement block or draw/graphicsLayer so only that phase re-runs; keep policies stable; avoid unneeded intrinsics and subcomposition.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
State read in composition → recompose + relayout. Read in measure → remeasure + replace. Read in placement → only placement re-runs. Read in draw lambda → redraw only. So animated offsets should use placeable.place { }/graphicsLayer {}/Modifier.offset { IntOffset } (lambda offset reads in layout phase) rather than Modifier.offset(x = animated.dp).

Allocation: measurables.map {} allocates a list per measure; fine for tens of children, harmful for hundreds in a scroll path. Alternatives: Array<Placeable?>, loops with index, remembering the policy via remember(params) { MeasurePolicy {...} } so Layout can skip remeasure when the policy is equal (a lambda recreated each recomposition counts as changed). For list children, don't write custom layout over 1000 items; use Lazy layouts.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Slider2(progress: () -> Float, content: @Composable () -> Unit) =
    Layout(content) { ms, c ->
        val p = ms[0].measure(c.copy(minWidth = 0, minHeight = 0))
        layout(c.maxWidth, p.height) {
            p.placeRelative(((c.maxWidth - p.width) * progress()).toInt(), 0) // read in placement only
        }
    }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Passing Float animated state down, reading in composition (every frame recomposes parents).
  • Recreating MeasurePolicy/lambdas capturing unstable values.
  • Per-measure sorting or groupBy.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you see it in a trace? → Compose:layout and measure slice duration; Layout Inspector recomposition counts.
  2. When is measure cached? → Layout node re-measures only if constraints or read state changed.
  3. How do you benchmark? → Macrobenchmark scrolling/animation with FrameTimingMetric.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior states the read-phase table and the lambda-based parameter pattern (progress: () -> Float).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A timeline view recomposed 60 times/s because the playhead float was read in composition; passing it as a lambda read in placement cut CPU in half (illustrative composite).

questions.promptHtml: How do you debug a layout that looks wrong, or find out which layouts are costly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks tool fluency rather than "I add colors to backgrounds".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Layout Inspector in Android Studio shows the composable tree with each node's size, constraints-derived bounds, modifiers and recomposition/skip counts, and a 3D view for overdraw and nesting. For cost, I take a system trace (Perfetto) and look at layout/measure slices; for a stable guard, a Macrobenchmark with FrameTimingMetric. Previews in multiple font scales/locales catch the rest.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Layout Inspector (Android Studio): attach to a running debuggable process; select a composable to see parameters and modifiers; enable recomposition counts (recomposed vs skipped). It shows bounds and the semantic/merged tree. Details of which fields are shown depend on Studio version (verify).
  • Perfetto / system trace: Compose emits trace sections for composition and layout when tracing is enabled; look for long measure/layout slices or nested subcomposition.
  • Compose compiler reports (-P plugin:androidx.compose.compiler.plugins.kotlin:reportsDestination=... for the older plugin; Kotlin 2.0 uses the Compose compiler Gradle plugin options, verify) for stability: not layout, but explains recomposition triggering relayout.
  • Modifier.border/background debug boxes, @Preview(fontScale=1.5f, locale="ar", showSystemUi=true).
  • Accessibility Scanner for touch target issues.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Preview(fontScale = 1.5f, locale = "ar", widthDp = 320)
@Composable
fun Stress() = AppTheme { OrderRow(sampleLongOrder) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Profiling a debug build.
  • Assuming recomposition count equals layout cost (layout can rerun without recomposition via state reads in measure).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to tell which phase re-ran? → Trace slices; recomposition counts only show composition.
  2. Debug constraints? → Temporary Modifier.layout { m, c -> Log.d("L", "$c"); ... } or inspect with the inspector.
  3. CI guard? → Screenshot tests at font scale/locales + macrobenchmark.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior separates composition, layout and draw and picks the right tool per phase.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "janky settings page" turned out to be one IntrinsicSize.Max visible only as a wide layout slice in Perfetto, not in recomposition counts.

questions.promptHtml: How does text get measured in Compose layouts, and when would you use TextMeasurer or onTextLayout?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Text is the main source of dynamic size; senior engineers need to reason about its cost and constraints.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Text measures during the layout pass using the incoming constraints: width bounds drive line wrapping, then height follows from lines. onTextLayout gives a TextLayoutResult (line count, overflow, baselines) after layout, for e.g. "read more". TextMeasurer lets you measure text outside composition/layout (for Canvas drawing or pre-sizing) using rememberTextMeasurer, with a cache.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Pipeline: Text → BasicText → text layout node whose measure builds paragraph layout (line breaking, shaping) for the width in constraints; result cached by params. Height depends on width, hence intrinsics for Text: minIntrinsicHeight(width) computes wrapped height; maxIntrinsicWidth = single-line width. Font scale and locale change lines and therefore sizes, so fixed-height containers clip at font scale 1.3+.

Cost: text layout is among the most expensive layout operations (shaping, line breaking); long strings in many items cost frame time. Avoid measuring the same text repeatedly: use rememberTextMeasurer(cacheSize = ...) and measure(...). Don't use onTextLayout to trigger state changes that alter layout every pass (relayout loop); use it for one-way decisions (e.g. hasVisualOverflow) with guarded state.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun ExpandableText(text: String) {
    var expanded by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
    var overflow by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
    Text(text, maxLines = if (expanded) Int.MAX_VALUE else 3, overflow = TextOverflow.Ellipsis,
        onTextLayout = { if (!expanded) overflow = it.hasVisualOverflow })
    if (overflow || expanded) TextButton({ expanded = !expanded }) { Text(if (expanded) "Less" else "More") }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Fixed-height rows with text, breaking at font scale 200%.
  • Writing state in onTextLayout unconditionally (extra recompositions).
  • TextMeasurer created in a loop without remember.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Autosizing text? → There's autoSize support in BasicText/Text in recent foundation versions (verify version); earlier, a measure loop with TextMeasurer.
  2. Why does Text in a Row with weight wrap oddly? → Constraint width from weight.
  3. Measuring text for 500 list items upfront? → Don't; measure lazily or cache; avoid layout-time measurement duplication.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior links text to constraints, intrinsics, and font scale, and treats it as the primary variable-size cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A chat bubble layout computed width with TextMeasurer per item per frame without caching; moving to cached measure fixed 3 ms frames (illustrative composite).

questions.contextHtml:
Two days after a release in 6 new locales (including German, Finnish, and Arabic), support tickets rise: "Pay button text cut off" and "price hidden". Telemetry: checkout completion fell 2.3 pts overall, 5.1 pts in de-DE; crash rate flat. Devices with system font scale >= 1.3 (about 22% of users) are the worst. Code:

Row(Modifier.fillMaxWidth().height(56.dp)) {
    Text(order.title, Modifier.fillMaxWidth(0.7f), maxLines = 1)
    Text(order.price, Modifier.weight(1f))
    Button(onClick = onPay, Modifier.height(40.dp)) { Text(stringResource(R.string.pay_now)) }
}

Screenshots show the button clipped vertically with German text wrapping to two lines.
questions.promptHtml: How do you triage and fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Shorten the German string" or "set maxLines = 1 everywhere".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it all locales or only long strings? Font scale distribution? Can we ship via staged rollout? Are translations final? Is the funnel drop in the button visible step?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix with flexible layout; temporary shorter copy via remote string override if available.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) fixed heights (56dp row, 40dp button) clip at font scale; (b) fillMaxWidth(0.7f) takes 70% of the Row's incoming width leaving 30% for price and button (fractions don't consider siblings); (c) button unweighted but measured after the 70% child, so it gets remaining space and wraps; (d) RTL red herring.
  4. How I'd verify: Previews with fontScale = 1.5f, locale = "de", widthDp 320; Layout Inspector on a device with large font; screenshot test matrix.
  5. Root cause: Constraint ordering plus fixed heights: first child demands 70%, the Button gets what's left and wraps its text, then clips in its fixed 40dp.
  6. Fix:
Row(Modifier.fillMaxWidth().heightIn(min = 56.dp), verticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically) {
    Text(order.title, Modifier.weight(1f), maxLines = 2, overflow = TextOverflow.Ellipsis)
    Spacer(Modifier.width(8.dp))
    Text(order.price)
    Spacer(Modifier.width(8.dp))
    Button(onClick = onPay) { Text(stringResource(R.string.pay_now)) }  // default min height, grows
}

Unweighted price and button are measured first so they never starve; title gets the remainder. 7. Prevention: Pseudolocale (en-XA) and font scale in screenshot tests; lint for fixed height with text; localization review with expansion factor. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't shrink fonts below accessibility sizes; don't hardcode sp text sizes via fontScale hacks; don't truncate the primary call to action.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Marketing demands one line button? → Allow maxLines=1 with autoSize where supported (verify), else restructure to a full-width bottom button.
  • Tablet? → Cap width with widthIn(max=).
  • Dynamic type 200%? → Switch to vertical layout via FlowRow/window size class check.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite fintech lost two weeks to "translation bugs" that were layout bugs; the fix was a font-scale screenshot gate.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: shortens copy.
  • Hire: removes fixed heights, fixes weight order.
  • Strong hire: explains measure order, builds test matrix, quantifies the funnel recovery plan.

questions.contextHtml: The "interest picker" screen uses a hand-written wrapping layout (like FlowRow) for 40 chips. The product now wants 400 chips (searchable tag cloud, 1M DAU, p50 device is a 3 GB phone). On the 400 chips, opening the screen takes 480 ms in layout alone and scrolling a verticalScroll Column containing it drops to 28 fps. The custom layout does measurables.map { it.measure(loose) } and then re-sorts children by width every pass. A teammate suggests IntrinsicSize.Min to "stabilize widths".
questions.promptHtml: How do you scale this?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Micro-optimizing the sort or adding remember blindly.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do all 400 need to be visible at once? Can the set be filtered/paged? Are chips selectable with animation? Is order fixed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap visible chips (top 40 + search), ship quickly.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) eager composition/measure of 400 children each pass; (b) sort per measure allocation; (c) intrinsic query traversal (not helpful; red herring, would add cost); (d) per-chip recomposition on selection change reading a shared set.
  4. How I'd verify: Perfetto layout slice; Macrobenchmark startup-to-interactive; Layout Inspector counts for selection toggles.
  5. Root cause: Non-lazy layout is O(n) per measure and each state change causes remeasure of all children; sorting adds O(n log n) allocations per pass.
  6. Fix: Short-term: remove sort (precompute order in the ViewModel), loop with indices, single pass; hoist selection to Set<Id> with derivedStateOf per chip. Long-term: virtualize: LazyVerticalStaggeredGrid/LazyVerticalGrid with adaptive cells or a lazy flow built on LazyColumn of precomputed rows (row breaking computed off main thread from measured/estimated chip widths using TextMeasurer).
  7. Prevention: Perf test with 10x data in CI; reviewers ask "does this layout scale with n?".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't use intrinsics here; don't hold 400 live subtree nodes if the user can't see them; precomputing rows needs consistent widths with font scale (recompute on config change).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Needs animated reorder? → animateItem() in lazy lists (verify modifier name for your version, formerly animateItemPlacement).
  • RTL? → Rows built with placeRelative/lazy handles it.
  • Selection toggles lag? → Per-item state and stable keys.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite app's tag screen went from 480 ms to 40 ms layout when rows were precomputed on a background dispatcher.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks code locally.
  • Hire: virtualizes with Lazy grid.
  • Strong hire: precomputes rows off-thread, handles font scale and RTL, adds a benchmark.

questions.contextHtml: PM asks: "Show three pricing cards side by side on tablets, all the same height regardless of text length, and stack them on phones." Cards contain a title, 2-8 feature lines (localized), and a CTA pinned to the bottom. You have a day for a design and a quick answer; the team debates IntrinsicSize.Max, fixed height(320.dp), or a custom layout.
questions.promptHtml: What do you decide, and what do you ask first?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Fixed height; or IntrinsicSize without understanding its scope.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is "tablet" (window width, foldable posture, split-screen)? Max feature count? Is localization or font scale in scope? Do the cards animate?
  2. Immediate mitigation: n/a; propose the simplest correct approach and its limits.
  3. Hypotheses (options) ranked: (a) Row with Modifier.height(IntrinsicSize.Max) and fillMaxHeight() cards: correct, cheap for 3 children; (b) fixed height: breaks localization/font scale; (c) custom layout: unnecessary unless intrinsics hurt.
  4. How I'd verify: Preview at fontScale 1.5, German, 600dp and 840dp widths; trace layout time (3 cards: negligible).
  5. Root cause: Equal height requires sibling knowledge = intrinsics or a custom layout; Row alone measures each child independently.
  6. Fix:
val wide = currentWindowAdaptiveInfo().windowSizeClass.isWidthAtLeastBreakpoint(WindowSizeClass.WIDTH_DP_MEDIUM_LOWER_BOUND) // verify API per adaptive version
if (wide) Row(Modifier.height(IntrinsicSize.Max), horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(16.dp)) {
    plans.forEach { PlanCard(it, Modifier.weight(1f).fillMaxHeight()) }
} else Column(verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(16.dp)) { plans.forEach { PlanCard(it) } }

Inside PlanCard use a Column with Spacer(Modifier.weight(1f)) before the CTA to pin it. 7. Prevention: Screenshot tests at three widths and font scales. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not fixed heights; not BoxWithConstraints per card; keep intrinsics to this small subtree; revisit if cards become lazy.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cards inside a LazyColumn? → Intrinsics inside item content is fine (not across the lazy boundary).
  • 12 plans? → Use a lazy grid with fixed rows, or custom layout to avoid intrinsics.
  • Very different aspect cards? → Allow max height cap heightIn(max=) and scroll inside.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team shipped fixed 320dp cards; German copy clipped the CTA below the fold on 20% of devices.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fixed heights.
  • Hire: intrinsics with justified scope.
  • Strong hire: window-size-based branching, pinned CTA, tests, and know when to switch to a custom layout.
